pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written nwt “the water-pot” or “the city” as a sky-determinative; the w is a weak consonant.
Feminine ending. Conventionally vocalised “Nut”. The name puns on nwt, “sky”.

pronunciation.note: The sky is grammatically feminine in Egyptian; her name is the sky-word itself.

domains.title: Goddess of the Sky, the Stars, and the Vault of Night
domains.subtitle: She Who Bends Over the Earth, Swallowing the Sun
domains.lead: Nwt is the sky — not a metaphor for it. Her body is the vault, starred across its length; her lips and womb the gates through which the sun passes at dusk and dawn. Each night she swallows the sun; each morning she gives birth to it again, the great cosmic rhythm painted on temple ceilings from Luxor to Dendera.

cards.name: The Starry Vault
cards.desc: Her body is painted blue across temple ceilings, scattered with the decans and planets she carries.

cards.name: Mother of the Gods
cards.desc: By Geb she bore Osiris, Isis, Seth, Nephthys, and Horus the Elder — the third generation of the Ennead.

cards.name: Swallower of the Sun
cards.desc: Each dusk the sun enters her mouth; each dawn she births it — time itself is her digestion.

cards.name: Lady of the Sycamore
cards.desc: She appears in tree-form pouring water and bread on the dead from a celestial sycamore.

mythology.lead: Nut enters myth chiefly as the forbidden wife: the sky and the earth, she and Geb, were locked in an embrace Shu had to tear apart to create the world’s space. Separated, she spends eternity arched over him, swallowing the sun he receives back each dawn — the most elegant creation image Egypt produced.

myths.title: The Embrace of Geb and Nut
myths.text: Shu and Tefnut, the first air and moisture, bore Geb the earth and Nut the sky — who loved so closely that no light or creature could pass between them. On Ra’s command, or by Shu’s own strength in the tellings, the air god forced them apart and holds them apart to this day: the atmosphere itself is the wedge of creation.

myths.title: The Birth Bricks of the Gods
myths.text: The old utterances make Nut the great mother repeatedly: she who bore the gods on her five epagomenal days — the days added outside the 360-day year, won for her from the moon in the game of senet. Osiris, Horus, Seth, Isis and Nephthys were born on those five days, the only time the sky goddess could labour.

myths.title: She Who Gives Birth and Does Not Tire
myths.text: Spell 17 invokes Nut as the sow who eats her piglets and the mother who daily bears the sun: ‘I am Nut, the great one who gives birth to the gods.’ The deceased appeals to her body as the ladder of ascent — to be ‘a star imperishable’ among her children was the standard hope of the afterlife.

myths.title: The Night Barque Within Her
myths.text: In the solar books the sun god’s night journey runs through Nut’s interior from mouth to womb; her body is the Duat’s architecture. New Kingdom royal tombs — from Thutmose III to Ramesses VI — paint her figure along the sarcophagus hall so that the king ascends through the goddess herself.

lore.syncretism: Nut merges readily with Hathor as sky-cow and with the sycamore-goddess of offering scenes; in the late period she absorbs the funerary role of Nut-as-tree. Greek authors rendered her as a Titaness-figure comparable to Rhea; her swallowing-and-birthing of the sun invited comparison with the devouring Time of Orphic cosmogonies.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her image — the blue woman bent from horizon to horizon — is the most reproduced Egyptian cosmological image after the weighing of the heart. The five epagomenal days her myth explains still structure the Coptic calendar’s year-end; and ‘Nut, Nut, the sky is falling’ passed into Egyptian Arabic as a children’s rhyme.
lore.extendedMeditation: A one-syllable name for the whole visible sky: nwt. To write it in ASCII is almost an act of honesty, for the word is a container — a water-pot determinative tipped onto its side — as if the Egyptians had already drawn the curve this temple builds its name upon. Her restoration needs no marks; the night sky over any city is her diacritic.

sources.name: Pyramid Texts (Nut as mother of the gods)
Book of the Dead, spells 17 and 148 (the Nut spell)
Temple ceiling programs: Dendera, Esna, Luxor
Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (epagomenal myth)

lore.archaeology: Her finest monuments are architectural: the ceilings of the Ramesside tombs in the Valley of the Kings and the zodiac ceiling of Dendera, where her body frames the circumpolar stars. The Nut spell (BD 148) was often written on stelae in the shape of the goddess herself, a tree-vault hybrid rising from the sycamore.
lore.cult: No single city claimed her exclusively — she was everyone’s sky — but she received royal cult in the mortuary temples and a popular cult as the sycamore who feeds the dead at the edge of desert necropolises. Her five epagomenal days closed the year with festival commotion everywhere.
lore.iconography: A naked or star-covered woman bent at the waist over the recumbent Geb, supported by Shu the air; or as a cow whose belly carries the sun-disc, four pillars of the sky beneath her legs. In the sycamore form she pours water from a jar over altars of the dead. Her headdress is the water-pot emblem that writes her name.
lore.reception: Through Plutarch she entered the classical imagination as one of the great mother-sky figures; Renaissance Hermeticism made her a standard emblem of the celestial vault. Modern Egyptology retains her as the canonical demonstration that Egyptian cosmology mapped theology directly onto visible nature.
